name: radiation oncology overview
title: Radiation therapy decision chart: radiate to cure a localized tumour (definitive or adjuvant, by external beam, brachytherapy or stereotactic beam) or to palliate a symptomatic one (urgent indications listed); then recognise toxicity by timing, acute during the course, subacute weeks later (pneumonitis treated with steroids) and late (hypothyroidism treated with replacement, infertility, second cancers)

root.title: Radiation: to CURE or to PALLIATE, and which TOXICITY do I watch for, and WHEN?
lines: damages DNA in normal and cancer cells alike → split into daily FRACTIONS (standard 1.8–2 Gy) so normal tissue repairs between them
every tissue has a TOLERANCE dose: spinal cord, bowel, kidney and lung often limit it · fast-growing tumours respond soonest

head: h
CURE
destroy a LOCALIZED tumour
what: • definitive: e.g. breast, prostate, lung, head and neck, lymphoma
• adjuvant: kill microscopic disease left after surgery or chemo
do: • external beam: 5 days a week, 1–10 weeks
• brachytherapy: isotope beside a gynecologic or prostate tumour
• stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR): very high dose in 1–5 treatments

head: h
PALLIATE
the tumour is causing SYMPTOMS
what: • bronchial or esophageal obstruction · gastrointestinal or gynecologic bleeding

head: h
ACUTE
during the course, by the site treated
what: • chest: esophagitis, cough · pelvis: diarrhea, urinary frequency
do: Expect them WORST near the END of the course

head: h
SUBACUTE
weeks later
what: 6–12 weeks after mediastinal radiation: fever, cough, dyspnea
• Lhermitte sign: tingling into the limbs on neck flexion

head: h
LATE
months to years
what: • infertility: sterile if > 2 Gy to the ovaries
• second cancers: large fields, > 40 Gy, older techniques
